title: AI finds tiny gene editor changes that reduce unintended DNA edits
excerpt: Gene editing is a highly precise and powerful technology that allows scientists to insert, delete, modify or replace DNA bases in living organisms. It has a variety of uses, including correcting disease-causing mutations and improving crops. Tools like CRISPR act as molecular scissors that target specific places in a genome to make these changes. But the technology is not perfect and can accidentally edit the wrong pieces of DNA or RNA.
content_html:
Gene editing is a highly precise and powerful technology that allows scientists to insert, delete, modify or replace DNA bases in living organisms. It has a variety of uses, including correcting disease-causing mutations and improving crops. Tools like CRISPR act as molecular scissors that target specific places in a genome to make these changes. But the technology is not perfect and can accidentally edit the wrong pieces of DNA or RNA.

In research published in Nature, scientists describe a new framework that uses AI to make these tools more accurate. Hoi Yee Chu and Alan S.L. Wong of the University of Hong Kong published a News and Views piece in the same journal on the significance of this research.

A new AI solution

Scientists from China developed an AI-guided platform to help redesign gene editors so they are more precise. It does this by using an AI program called AlphaFold3.

This system predicts how strongly different biological molecules are likely to interact with one another. When a gene editor enters a cell, it has to bind to a specific piece of target DNA. AlphaFold3 works by predicting the probability that amino acids in the gene-editing protein will come into close contact with the target DNA and the guide RNA that directs the editor.

By comparing these contact probabilities between intended and unintended DNA targets, the platform can identify the parts of a gene editor that contribute to accidental edits. This differs from the current approach, which considers the 3D shapes of the editor and DNA molecules to spot errors.

"ContactSeek represents a computational approach for enhancing the specificity of genome editors," the scientists wrote in their paper. "CP is a more sensitive output than predicted 3D structure for discerning differential interactions."

Improving precision

The study authors tested ContactSeek on an adenine base editor, a type of gene editor that fixes single-letter typos in DNA. The AI analyzed the tool's mistakes and suggested tiny corrections. When these were made, the upgraded version reduced genome-wide off-target editing by about 83% for one of the guide RNAs tested. The platform also helped improve the accuracy of a different type of gene editor, a Cas12a-based cytosine-based editor.

ContactSeek is not yet ready for clinical use because further tests in different cell types and genome targets are needed. But when it is ready, the research team envisions it being widely used.

"We anticipate that ContactSeek ... will be broadly applicable to a wide range of DNA- and RNA-editing tools," said the researchers.

content_html_zh:
基因编辑是一项高度精确且强大的技术，使科学家能够在生物体中插入、删除、修改或替换 DNA 碱基。 它有多种用途，包括纠正致病突变和改良作物。 CRISPR 等工具就像分子剪刀一样，针对基因组中的特定位置进行这些改变。 但这项技术并不完美，可能会意外编辑错误的 DNA 或 RNA 片段。

在《自然》杂志上发表的研究中，科学家描述了一个新的框架，该框架使用人工智能来使这些工具更加准确。 海怡珠和 Alan S.L. 香港大学的黄在同一期刊上发表了一篇新闻与观点文章，阐述了这项研究的意义。

新的人工智能解决方案

中国科学家开发了一个人工智能引导平台，帮助重新设计基因编辑器，使其更加精确。 它通过使用名为 AlphaFold3 的人工智能程序来实现这一点。

该系统可以预测不同的生物分子之间相互作用的强度。 当基因编辑器进入细胞时，它必须与特定的目标 DNA 片段结合。 AlphaFold3 的工作原理是预测基因编辑蛋白中的氨基酸与目标 DNA 和指导编辑器的向导 RNA 紧密接触的概率。

通过比较预期和非预期 DNA 目标之间的接触概率，该平台可以识别基因编辑器中导致意外编辑的部分。 这与当前的方法不同，当前的方法考虑编辑器和 DNA 分子的 3D 形状来发现错误。

科学家们在论文中写道：“ContactSeek 代表了一种增强基因组编辑特异性的计算方法。” “对于辨别差异相互作用而言，CP 是比预测的 3D 结构更敏感的输出。”

提高精度

研究作者在腺嘌呤碱基编辑器上测试了 ContactSeek，腺嘌呤碱基编辑器是一种基因编辑器，可以修复 DNA 中的单字母拼写错误。 人工智能分析了该工具的错误并提出了微小的修正建议。 当这些完成后，升级版本将测试的指导 RNA 之一的全基因组脱靶编辑减少了约 83%。 该平台还有助于提高不同类型基因编辑器（基于 Cas12a 的胞嘧啶编辑器）的准确性。

ContactSeek 尚未准备好用于临床，因为需要对不同细胞类型和基因组目标进行进一步测试。 但当它准备就绪时，研究团队预计它会被广泛使用。

“我们预计 ContactSeek ... 将广泛适用于各种 DNA 和 RNA 编辑工具，”研究人员说。
